## Statement

For every tagged scalable compound $c$, the mass in [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] is independent of the finite summation set used. For any compounds $c,d$ and $t\ge0$, $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$ and $m(tc)=t m(c)$; $m(0)=0$. For every $x\in X$, the unit-state compound $e_x$ has $m(e_x)=1$. A compound has zero mass if and only if it is the empty compound.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]: compounds are nonnegative finite-support functions, and mass is defined by a finite sum over support.

[F2] [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]] supplies bijective reindexing and splitting over disjoint finite sets. Enumerating a finite set expresses its real sum using [[def-finite-sum]]; additivity and scalar linearity then follow from clauses 1 and 2 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. In particular, its sum of zero terms is zero, so disjoint splitting shows that adjoining zero terms leaves a sum unchanged. Clause 4 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] gives nonnegativity of a sum of nonnegative terms and says that a zero sum forces each term to be zero.

## Proof

**Given:** [F1] and [F2].

1.1 Let $E$ be any finite subset of $X$ containing $\operatorname{supp}(c)$. On $E\setminus\operatorname{supp}(c)$ the function is zero, so the finite sum over $E$ equals the finite sum over $\operatorname{supp}(c)$ by [F2]. If $E$ and $E'$ both contain the support, compare each sum to the sum over the finite union $E\cup E'$; hence the value is independent of the chosen finite summation set. [F1, F2]

2.1 The support of $c+d$ is contained in the finite union of the supports of $c$ and $d$. Sum over that union; distributivity in [F2] gives $m(c+d)=m(c)+m(d)$, since zero terms outside each individual support contribute nothing by step 1.1. The support of $tc$ equals that of $c$ for $t>0$, and scalar linearity of the finite sum gives $m(tc)=t m(c)$. For $t=0$, $tc=0$ and both $m(tc)$ and $t m(c)$ are zero. The empty sum is zero, so $m(0)=0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The support of $e_x$ is the singleton $\{x\}$, whose one summand is $1$, so the recursion in [F2] gives $m(e_x)=0+1=1$. If $m(c)=0$, sum its nonnegative coefficients over its finite support. Clause 4 in [F2] forces every summand to be zero; coefficients off the support are also zero, hence $c=0$. Conversely $c=0$ has zero mass by step 2.1. Thus all the claimed mass identities hold, including the empty and unit-state cases. [F1, F2, step 2.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $P$ be a set of primitive type labels. A formal type $\Gamma$ records a finitely supported amount function $\nu_\Gamma:P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$, not identically zero. Primitive generators have their unit amount function. Positive scaling, separated product, and thermal-join constructors retain distinct formal tags and obey

$$\nu_{s\Gamma}=s\nu_\Gamma,\qquad \nu_{\Gamma\otimes\Gamma'}=\nu_\Gamma+\nu_{\Gamma'}\qquad(s>0).$$

Separated and joined types are distinct constructors even when their amount functions agree. Permutation, reassociation, and scaled-splitting conventions preserve the amount function. Define the positive **bookkeeping weight** $w_\Gamma:=\sum_{p\in P}\nu_\Gamma(p)$, a finite sum over support. Thus $w_{s\Gamma}=s w_\Gamma$ and every product or join has weight $w_\Gamma+w_{\Gamma'}$. The optional empty unit has zero amount function and weight zero; it is represented only by the empty compound, not as a simple chart. These are formal amounts, not masses in kilograms or an empirical conservation law. The functions and pointwise operations use [[def-function-space]]; their finite-support convention and finite sums are those of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]].

For Euclidean vectors use $a\cdot b=\sum_j a_jb_j$ and $\|a\|=(a\cdot a)^{1/2}$. Write $B(a,r)=\{b:\|b-a\|<r\}$. Open means each point has such a ball contained in the set; convex means $(1-t)a+tb$ belongs to the set for all its $a,b$ and $0\le t\le1$. In a subspace or subset, use intersections of these balls for the relative topology. A map $P:D\to\mathbb R^n$ is locally Lipschitz if each $a\in D$ has a relative neighborhood $V$ and finite $L\ge0$ with $\|P(b)-P(c)\|\le L\|b-c\|$ for all $b,c\in V$. A set $D$ is arcwise connected here if each two distinct points are joined by a continuous injective map $\gamma:[0,1]\to D$ with those endpoints; singleton and empty sets satisfy this condition vacuously. Continuity uses the indicated Euclidean relative topology. Let $I$ index the declared family of simple types $\Gamma_i$. For each simple type $\Gamma$ in that family, let $n_\Gamma\ge1$ and let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n_\Gamma+1}$ be nonempty, open and convex, with coordinates $x=(u,v)$. The notation for a type and its chart is shared, but each state has a distinct raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$. Scaled charts are distinct tagged copies $s\Gamma=\{sx:x\in\Gamma\}$ with coordinate transport $x\mapsto sx$; transported raw tags remain distinct from the original raw tags. Let $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$ be the unit point mass from [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. The represented state is

$$\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x):=w_\Gamma e_{(\Gamma,x)},\qquad m(\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))=w_\Gamma.$$

Write $\mathsf{J}(x):=\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ when $x$ already carries its type tag. All state notation in this framework's compound comparisons, including a bare $x$, denotes $\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$; a raw unit point mass is always written $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. A separated pair is addition of represented states, not a unit product tag. Nonnegative multiples are pointwise and zero terms are omitted. For an encoded compound $c$, its aggregate composition is the finite amount function

$$\nu(c):=\sum_{(\Gamma,x)\in\operatorname{supp}(c)}\frac{c(\Gamma,x)}{w_\Gamma}\nu_\Gamma;\qquad m(c)=\sum_{p\in P}\nu(c)(p).$$

Fix the formal interpretation $\Pi(c)$ as the finite separated preparation whose factor at each nonzero raw tag $(\Gamma,x)$ is the amount $c(\Gamma,x)/w_\Gamma$ of that typed state, using the declared coordinate scaling transport. Let $\mathcal P:=\{\Pi(c):c\text{ is a finite nonnegative encoded compound}\}$ be the set of these preparations, with an invariant bookkeeping mass $M:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ satisfying $M(\Pi(c))=m(c)$. As additional model data choose a binary relation $Q\subseteq\{(p,q)\in\mathcal P^2:M(p)=M(q)\}$. Define its pullback on encoded compounds by $A\prec B$ if and only if $(\Pi(A),\Pi(B))\in Q$. The transport, reversibility and A1–A7 assumptions below constrain this chosen relation; they do not construct it from coordinates. Merging or splitting repeated copies of the same preparation is reversible; permutation and reassociation preserve the preparation. Thus $\Pi(\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx))$ and $\Pi(s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x))$ are the same declared scaled preparation and yield

$$\mathsf{J}_{s\Gamma}(sx)\sim s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x),$$

although their raw point masses have different tags and are not equal. This reversible transport commutes with finite composition, nested type constructors, and scaled splitting. It is part of the precise formal scaling interpretation, not a deduction about physical accessibility from coordinate multiplication. A physical use must adopt the stated preparation maps and accessibility assumptions; fixed-composition models compare only preparations with the same $\nu$, while a declared channel model may additionally compare different compositions of equal $m$.

This Definition restricts comparisons $A\prec B$ to $m(A)=m(B)$; the coefficient-map supplier defines the mass, not the comparison relation. Write $A\sim B$ when both directions hold, and $A\prec\prec B$ when only the forward direction holds. On any fixed simple type, dividing every represented state by the same positive constant $w_\Gamma$ gives its unit-point-mass comparison. Positive scaling and its inverse preserve and reflect order; whenever the required CH and reference hypotheses hold, the unit-state entropy theorem applies after that normalization. If $S$ represents unit-point-mass comparisons, the entropy of a represented state is $w_\Gamma S(x)$ and the entropy of a finite sum $\sum_j t_j\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x_j)$ is $\sum_j t_j w_\Gamma S(x_j)$. No independent rescaling across different types is assumed without a calibrator.

The common relation satisfies A1–A6 on all equal-mass finite compounds: (A1) reflexivity; (A2) transitivity; (A3) if $A\prec B$, then $A+C\prec B+C$ for every compound $C$; (A4) if $A\prec B$, then $tA\prec tB$ for every $t>0$; (A5) $t\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ is equivalent to $s\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)+(t-s)\mathsf{J}_\Gamma(x)$ for $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, with the reversible scaled-copy transport above; (A6) for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive equal-mass spectators $Z_0,Z_1$, and every sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to zero, $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\prec B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for all $n$ implies $A\prec B$. These are hypotheses, not conclusions. No comparison hypothesis is included here.

For each $i$ and $x\in\Gamma_i$, define the forward sector $A_x:=\{y\in\Gamma_i:\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)\prec\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)\}$. The simple-domain assumptions are: (A7) for $x,y\in\Gamma_i$ and $0<t<1$, the encoded compound $t\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+(1-t)\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(y)$ compares to $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(tx+(1-t)y)$; both have bookkeeping mass $w_{\Gamma_i}$, and convexity puts the recombined coordinate in the chart; (S1) each $x$ has a strict successor; (S2) $A_x$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$, expressible as $u-u_x+P_i(x)\cdot(v-v_x)=0$ with a finite-valued slope map $P_i:\Gamma_i\to\mathbb R^{n_i}$, and $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz; (S3) the boundary of $A_x$ relative to $\Gamma_i$ is arcwise connected. A supporting hyperplane means that $A_x$ lies in one of its closed half-spaces and meets the plane at $x$. The affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing a set; relative interior is interior in that affine hull. Closure and boundary are taken in the indicated affine hull or in $\Gamma_i$, as named; boundary is closure intersected with closure of the complement in that relative topology.

This definition imposes no physical interpretation, units, or empirical claim. A contact theorem that uses joins must separately assume that each join is a simple domain satisfying these same forward-sector hypotheses.

## Definition

For two simple domains $\Gamma_i\subset\mathbb R^{n_i+1}$ and $\Gamma_j\subset\mathbb R^{n_j+1}$, write their coordinates $(u_i,v_i)$ and $(u_j,v_j)$. Their thermal-join domain is

$$\Delta_{ij}:=\{(u,v_i,v_j):\exists u_i,u_j,\ (u_i,v_i)\in\Gamma_i,\ (u_j,v_j)\in\Gamma_j,\ u=u_i+u_j\}.$$

The joined simple type is a distinct formal tag with amount function $\nu_{\Delta_{ij}}=\nu_{\Gamma_i}+\nu_{\Gamma_j}$ and weight $w_{\Delta_{ij}}=w_{\Gamma_i}+w_{\Gamma_j}$, as defined in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Encode the separated pair by $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and a joined coordinate $Z$ by $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(Z)$. Their bookkeeping masses agree, and their aggregate composition functions agree. These encoded maps and their raw tags remain distinct. Positive coordinate-scaled copies use the reversible preparation transport of that definition; nested joins preserve their finite primitive amount function under reassociation and permutation. The empty type contributes the zero map.

Write $J_{ij}(x,y)$ for the join state with the summed energy coordinate and the unchanged work coordinates. A compound pair $(x,y)$ and $J_{ij}(x,y)$ have the same total energy and work coordinates but are distinct tagged objects. Define $x\sim_T y$ exactly when $\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x)+\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_j}(y)$ and $\mathsf{J}_{\Delta_{ij}}(J_{ij}(x,y))$ are accessible in both directions. Nested joins use the declared reassociation and permutation identifications.

Assume every finite join is itself a simple domain satisfying [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. The contact hypotheses are mathematical assumptions on the common relation: (T1) $(x,y)\prec J_{ij}(x,y)$; (T2) every join state has at least one reversible split into component states at its stated coordinates, and the equal-state split of any state into positive scaled copies of itself is reversible; (T3) $\sim_T$ is transitive; (T4) for every simple state $x$ there are states $x_0,x_1$ in its domain with $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ and $x_0\sim_T x_1$; (T5) for every ordered pair of simple systems, every $x$ in the first and every work coordinate $v$ in the second's projection $\rho(\Gamma_j):=\{v:\exists u,(u,v)\in\Gamma_j\}$, there is a state $y$ with work coordinate $v$ and $x\sim_T y$.

For the completed calibrator branch, add (C1) **join coherence**: whenever $x\sim_T y$, the join state $J_{ij}(x,y)$ is thermally equivalent to each of $x$ and $y$ under the nested-join identifications. The coordinate sum in the definition alone does not assert C1. In later theorem statements, T1–T5 and C1 are explicitly listed as hypotheses; they are not treated as established physical laws.

## Statement refuted

The coordinate set formula for a thermal join, without an accessibility or thermal-equilibrium specification, forces C1 join coherence.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The coordinate formula for a join, with no interpretation of accessibility or thermal equivalence imposed by that formula.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]: the join domain is determined by the coordinate sum $u=u_1+u_2$, while C1 is a separate relation-level assumption.

## Counterexample

1.1 Start with a primitive tag $g$ and close it under the ordered binary join constructor $(T,R)\mapsto T\vee R$, retaining a distinct tag for each finite binary tree. Let $n_T\ge1$ count its primitive leaves, give it amount $n_T$ of the one primitive label and weight $n_T$, and set $\Gamma_T=\mathbb R^{n_T+1}$ with one energy and $n_T$ work coordinates. Define $J_{T,R}((u,v),(u',v'))=(u+u',v,v')$ in the distinct tagged chart $\Gamma_{T\vee R}$. Since $n_{T\vee R}=n_T+n_R$ and energies range over all reals, this chart has exactly the join coordinate-set formula. Reassociation and permutation use the corresponding energy-preserving permutations of work coordinates. Encode a state by $\mathsf J_T(x)=n_T e_{(T,x)}$; separated pairs and joins have equal mass but different raw supports. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 On finite encoded compounds define accessibility as the smallest equivalence relation containing, for every $x\in\Gamma_g$, the pair $2e_{(g,x)}$ and $2e_{(g\vee g,J_{g,g}(x,x))}$. Each generating pair has mass two, so every class at any other mass is a singleton; all comparisons have equal mass. Define $\sim_T$ by [F1]'s mutual-accessibility rule for the separated pair and its joined state. Fix $x\in\Gamma_g$ and put $z=J_{g,g}(x,x)$. The generating pair gives $x\sim_T x$. But testing $z\sim_T x$ compares $2e_{(g\vee g,z)}+e_{(g,x)}$ with $3e_{((g\vee g)\vee g,J_{g\vee g,g}(z,x))}$. These distinct mass-three compounds lie in distinct singleton classes. Thus $z\not\sim_T x$, so C1 fails. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 On the same tagged charts and encodings, instead make every pair of equal-mass compounds accessible. The supplier's mutual-accessibility rule now makes every thermal comparison true, so C1 holds with exactly the same coordinate formula. These models test only the implication from bare join coordinates; neither is asserted to satisfy all forward-sector, geometric or contact axioms. Both realize thermal equivalence through an actual compound relation. Their different C1 outcomes show that the coordinate data alone do not force coherence. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement refuted

At fixed activity $z>0$ and inverse temperature $\beta>0$, adding any spatially constant one-particle external energy throughout a continuum ideal-gas region leaves the thermodynamic-limit log grand partition sum per volume unchanged, as would a negligible boundary perturbation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $V>0$, $z>0$, $\beta>0$, constant $c\in\mathbb R$, and the $1/N!$-normalized positional grand sum.

[A1] The model has zero pair energy and assigns each $N$-point configuration external energy $cN$.

[F1] [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], and [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: the product coordinate integral of the constant one over $\Omega^N$ is $V^N$.

[F2] [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], and [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]: the nonnegative exponential series satisfies $\sum_{N\geq0}x^N/N!=e^x$.

## Counterexample

**Given:** $V>0$, $z>0$, $\beta>0$, constant $c\in\mathbb R$, and the $1/N!$-normalized positional grand sum.

For the continuum ideal gas in a bounded measurable region $\Omega$ of volume $V$, use activity $z>0$, inverse temperature $\beta>0$, and no pair interaction. Add a constant external one-particle energy $c$ throughout $\Omega$. This volume-sized field changes the pressure per volume whenever $c\ne0$, so it is not a negligible boundary perturbation.

1.1 The $N$-particle term without the field is $z^NV^N/N!$, by the product volume [F1] and the $1/N!$ convention [given]. Summing over $N\geq0$ gives $\Xi_0=\sum_N(zV)^N/N!=e^{zV}$ by [F2]. [given, A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 With the field, each term is multiplied by $e^{-\beta cN}$, so $\Xi_c=\sum_N(ze^{-\beta c}V)^N/N!=e^{ze^{-\beta c}V}$ by [F2]. Therefore $V^{-1}\log\Xi_0=z$ and $V^{-1}\log\Xi_c=ze^{-\beta c}$. If $c\ne0$, these differ because $z,\beta>0$. [given, A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open, $n\ge1$, with coordinates $(x_1,\ldots,x_n,z)$. For $k\in\{1,2\}$, a $C^k$ one-form on $U$ is a field of linear functionals on tangent vectors of the form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i(x,z)\,dx_i+b(x,z)\,dz$, where every coefficient is $k$ times continuously differentiable. At $q\in U$, it acts by $\omega_q(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)=\sum_i a_i(q)u_i+b(q)w$. It is nonsingular on $U$ when $\omega_q\ne0$ for every $q$; then $H_q:=\ker\omega_q$ is an $n$-dimensional subspace of $T_qU\cong\mathbb R^{n+1}$.

For a $C^1$ scalar function $S:W\to\mathbb R$ on an open $W\subseteq U$, its differential is the one-form defined by

$$dS_q(v):=DS(q)v=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_{x_i}S(q)u_i+\partial_zS(q)w,\qquad v=(u_1,\ldots,u_n,w)\in T_qW.$$

In particular, if $S\in C^2(W)$, then $dS$ is a $C^1$ one-form.

For one-forms $\alpha,\beta$, their exterior product is the alternating two-form $(\alpha\wedge\beta)(u,v)=\alpha(u)\beta(v)-\alpha(v)\beta(u)$. For a one-form $\alpha$ and a two-form $\sigma$, $(\alpha\wedge\sigma)(u,v,w)=\alpha(u)\sigma(v,w)-\alpha(v)\sigma(u,w)+\alpha(w)\sigma(u,v)$. For a $C^1$ one-form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,dx_i+b\,dz$, its exterior derivative is the continuous two-form

$$d\omega=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dx_j+\sum_{i=1}^n(\partial_i b-\partial_z a_i)\,dx_i\wedge dz.$$

When $\omega$ is $C^2$, the coefficients of $d\omega$ are $C^1$.

For a $C^2$ one-form on this page, the codimension-one Pfaff condition means the pointwise equation $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$.

A piecewise-$C^1$ path is a continuous $\gamma:[s_0,s_1]\to U$ with $s_0\le s_1$ and admitting a finite partition on each closed subinterval of which it is $C^1$. It is $\omega$-horizontal when $\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))=0$ on the interior of each such subinterval. Endpoints where a derivative is one-sided are included by continuity. For an open $V\subseteq U$, $p$ is horizontally reachable from $q$ within $V$ if a horizontal path in $V$ joins $q$ to $p$. Both signs of time and finite concatenations are allowed by this definition.

On a neighborhood $W$, an integrating factor for $\omega$ is a nowhere-zero $\mu\in C^1(W)$ for which $\mu\omega=dS$ for some $S\in C^2(W)$ with $dS$ nowhere zero. This definition is local; it asserts neither a global potential on $U$ nor a physical identification or calibration of $S$.

## Statement refuted

Every closed $C^1$ one-form on every connected open domain in $\mathbb R^2$ is globally exact.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Here closed means $d\omega=0$ by the coordinate formula, and exact means $\omega=dS$ for a globally defined $C^2$ scalar function $S$ on the stated open domain.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-one-form-and-horizontal-path]]: the coordinate formula for $d\omega$ and the coordinate action of a one-form.

[F2] [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]: for $F=(P,Q)$ and a piecewise-$C^1$ curve $\gamma$, $\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r=\int(P(\gamma)\gamma'_1+Q(\gamma)\gamma'_2)\,dt$.

[F3] [[thm-gradient-theorem-for-line-integrals]]: if $F=\nabla S$ on an open set, its line integral along $\gamma$ is $S(\gamma(1))-S(\gamma(0))$.

[F4] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]] and [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: continuous integrands are Riemann integrable, and $\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi$.

## Counterexample

1.1 Let $D=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ and $\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy$ with $P(x,y)=-y/(x^2+y^2)$ and $Q(x,y)=x/(x^2+y^2)$. The domain $D$ is open since each nonzero point has a ball avoiding the origin. The coefficient vector $(P,Q)=(-y,x)/(x^2+y^2)$ is nonzero at every point of $D$. The domain is path-connected: if the segment joining $p,q\in D$ avoids $0$, use that segment; if it contains $0$, then $p,q,0$ are collinear. Writing $p=(p_1,p_2)$, take $r=(-p_2,p_1)$; it is nonzero and perpendicular to $p$, so $p,r$ and $q,r$ are linearly independent pairs and the segments $[p,r]$ and $[r,q]$ avoid $0$. [given, F1]

2.1 Write $r^2=x^2+y^2>0$. For sufficiently small $h$, direct difference quotients give $\partial_xP=2xy/r^4$, $\partial_yQ=-2xy/r^4$, and $\partial_xQ=\partial_yP=(y^2-x^2)/r^4$: for example, $\bigl(Q(x+h,y)-Q(x,y)\bigr)/h=(y^2-x^2-xh)/(r^2((x+h)^2+y^2))$ and $\bigl(P(x,y+h)-P(x,y)\bigr)/h=(y^2-x^2+yh)/(r^2(x^2+(y+h)^2))$, while the other two quotients are $y(2x+h)/(r^2((x+h)^2+y^2))$ and $-x(2y+h)/(r^2(x^2+(y+h)^2))$. These limits are continuous on $D$, so $P,Q\in C^1(D)$; the cross partials agree and the coordinate definition [F1] gives $d\omega=(\partial_xQ-\partial_yP)dx\wedge dy=0$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The unit circle $\gamma(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$, $0\le t\le2\pi$, lies in the domain and uses the form defined in step 1.1. Along it $(P,Q)=(-\sin t,\cos t)=\gamma'(t)$, hence [F2] gives $\int_\gamma\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi$ by [F4]. [F2, F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 The closedness is proved in step 2.1. If $\omega=dS$ globally on $D$, then $F=\nabla S$ for the corresponding vector field, and [F3] would give $\int_\gamma\omega=S(\gamma(2\pi))-S(\gamma(0))=0$, contradicting step 2.2. Thus $\omega$ is closed but not globally exact. This does not assert that every possible global integrating factor is absent. [F3, step 2.1, step 2.2, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Statement

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be open. Let $\omega$ be a $C^1$ one-form on $U$, $\mu\in C^1(U)$ nowhere zero, and $S\in C^2(U)$ with $dS=\mu\omega$. Then $\omega\wedge d\omega=0$ on $U$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated open domain, regularity, and identity $dS=\mu\omega$.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-one-form-and-horizontal-path]]: exterior differentiation is coordinate antisymmetrized partial differentiation, and $\wedge$ is the alternating exterior product.

[F2] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: coordinate compositions with line segments obey the total-derivative chain rule.

[F3] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]] and [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: continuous partial derivatives are integrable on coordinate intervals, and their interval integrals give endpoint differences.

[F4] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] and [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]]: a closed coordinate rectangle is compact and continuous second partials on it are uniformly continuous.

## Proof

**Given:** The stated $\omega,\mu,S$; write $S_i=\partial_iS$ in Euclidean coordinates.

1.1 Fix $q\in U$ and distinct coordinates $i,j$. Choose $h,k>0$ small enough that the coordinate rectangle from $q$ to $q+he_i+ke_j$ lies in $U$, and set $\Delta=S(q+he_i+ke_j)-S(q+he_i)-S(q+ke_j)+S(q)$. By [F4] the second partials are uniformly continuous on the chosen closed rectangle. Applying [F2] to coordinate segments and [F3] to their continuous derivatives, Newton–Leibniz gives
$$\Delta=\int_0^h\!\int_0^k S_{ij}(q+se_i+te_j)\,dt\,ds=\int_0^k\!\int_0^h S_{ji}(q+se_i+te_j)\,ds\,dt.$$
Each equality follows by taking the two endpoint differences in the outer coordinate and then applying Newton–Leibniz to the inner difference; both integrands are continuous by $S\in C^2$. [F2, F3, F4]

2.1 Divide both expressions in step 1.1 by $hk$ and let $h,k\downarrow0$. Continuity of $S_{ij}$ and $S_{ji}$ makes each average tend to its value at $q$, so $S_{ij}(q)=S_{ji}(q)$. Since $q,i,j$ were arbitrary, the coordinate formula in [F1] gives $d(dS)=0$. [step 1.1, F1, F4, algebra]

3.1 Put $\lambda:=1/\mu$. Total differentiability gives $\mu(q+h)=\mu(q)+D\mu(q)h+o(\|h\|)$, and continuity with $\mu(q)\ne0$ gives $\mu(q+h)\mu(q)=\mu(q)^2+o(1)$. Hence $\lambda(q+h)-\lambda(q)=-\bigl(\mu(q+h)-\mu(q)\bigr)/\bigl(\mu(q+h)\mu(q)\bigr)=-\mu(q)^{-2}D\mu(q)h+o(\|h\|)$, so $\lambda\in C^1(U)$ with continuous derivative $D\lambda=-\mu^{-2}D\mu$. For each $i$, $S_i=\partial_i S$ is $C^1$. ## Definition

Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset of $\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, with its Borel sigma-algebra, and let $a:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. The **convex hull** $\operatorname{conv}K$ is the set of finite convex combinations of points of $K$. A **phase generator** is a point $y\in K$ with declared energy $a(y)$. A **mixture** is a Borel probability measure $P$ on $K$. Its barycenter and mean energy are the coordinatewise Lebesgue integrals
$$\bar y(P):=\int_K y\,dP(y)\in\mathbb R^d,\qquad \bar a(P):=\int_K a(y)\,dP(y)\in\mathbb R.$$
These integrals are finite because each coordinate and $a$ are bounded on compact $K$. For prescribed mean $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$, the **mixture energy** is
$$a_{\rm mix}(x):=\inf\{\bar a(P):P\text{ is a Borel probability on }K,\ \bar y(P)=x\}.$$
The admissible set is nonempty since every finite convex combination of points of $K$ is the barycenter of a finite atomic probability. The definition does not assert that the infimum is attained; the theorem on this page gives a compact continuous sufficient condition.

## Scope

The definition concerns a mathematical probability mixture and an assigned scalar energy. It does not assert that physical phases can be prepared, exchanged, or brought to equilibrium.

## Statement

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty compact, $d\ge1$, and $a:K\to\mathbb R$ continuous. Define $a_{\rm mix}$ as in [[def-tdmath-mixture-generator-space-and-energy]]. Then for every $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$ the infimum defining $a_{\rm mix}(x)$ is attained by a Borel probability measure supported on at most $d+1$ points. The function $a_{\rm mix}$ is lower semicontinuous and convex on $\operatorname{conv}K$, and is the greatest convex function on $\operatorname{conv}K$ bounded above by $a$ on $K$. Minimizing over all Borel probabilities on $K$ gives the same attained value as minimizing over finite mixtures. This is a mathematical compactness result; it makes no phase-preparation or equilibrium postulate.

**Given:** The compact generator space, continuous energy, and Borel-probability mixture convention.

## Statement refuted

Every nonzero-time map of a complete Hamiltonian flow preserving finite symplectic volume is ergodic with respect to the normalized volume measure.

## Definition

Fix a nonempty set $X$ and the compounds of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]. A **comparison relation** $\preceq$ is defined only for pairs $(A,B)$ with $m(A)=m(B)$. Write $A\sim B$ when both $A\preceq B$ and $B\preceq A$; this is equivalence, not equality of coefficient functions. The following are explicit hypotheses on $\preceq$:

1. **Preorder:** $A\preceq A$, and $A\preceq B\preceq C$ implies $A\preceq C$.
2. **Composition consistency:** $A\preceq B$ implies $A+C\preceq B+C$ for every compound $C$.
3. **Positive scaling:** $A\preceq B$ implies $tA\preceq tB$ for every real $t>0$.
4. **Splitting and recombination:** for $x\in X$, $t>0$ and $0<s<t$, the one-state compound $te_x$ is equivalent to $se_x+(t-s)e_x$.
5. **Stability:** for equal-mass $A,B$, fixed positive compounds $Z_0,Z_1$ with $m(Z_0)=m(Z_1)$, and a sequence $\epsilon_n>0$ decreasing to $0$, if $A+\epsilon_n Z_0\preceq B+\epsilon_n Z_1$ for every $n$, then $A\preceq B$.
6. **Comparison hypothesis (CH):** for every equal-mass pair $A,B$, either $A\preceq B$ or $B\preceq A$ (or both).

These are mathematical assumptions, not conclusions about a physical system. No antisymmetry, continuity, convexity, or strict comparison is included. Strict comparison means $A\preceq B$ and not $B\preceq A$.

## Remarks

In the stability clause, a sequence $\epsilon_n$ is a function $\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$; “decreasing to $0$” means $\epsilon_m\le\epsilon_n$ whenever $n\le m$ and $\epsilon_n\to0$ in the sense of [[def-real-limit]]. The separate requirement $\epsilon_n>0$ is stated in the clause.

## Definition

Let $u,v:X\to\mathbb R$ be finite-support real coefficient maps with equal total coefficient $\sum_xu(x)=\sum_xv(x)$. These signed maps are formal comparison notation, not compounds. Put $d:=v-u$ and define $d^+(x):=\max\{d(x),0\}$ and $d^-(x):=\max\{-d(x),0\}$. Then $d^+,d^-$ are nonnegative finite-support compounds of equal mass, as verified in [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]. Define

$$u\preceq_s v\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d^-\preceq d^+,$$

using the compound comparison relation of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]. Thus positive coefficients of $v-u$ remain on the right and negative coefficients move to the left. Signed notation is never a claim that a negative amount of a physical system exists.

## Statement

In the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$, the sequence $\epsilon_n:=1/(n+1)$, $n\in\mathbb N$, is positive, strictly decreasing, and converges to zero.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: every nonempty subset of an ordered field that is bounded above has a least upper bound.

[F2] [[def-natural-numbers]], [[def-nat-addition]], [[lem-nat-add-commutative]], [[lem-nat-add-identity]], and [[def-nat-order]]: $\mathbb N$ is the von Neumann set of naturals, its successor is $\sigma(n)=n+1$, and $m\le n$ means $m+k=n$ for some $k\in\mathbb N$. Since $1+n=n+1=\sigma(n)$, every successor is at least $1$. Natural indices remain in $\mathbb N$; in field expressions the successor is carried into $\mathbb R$ by the canonical natural map of [[def-canonical-natural]].

[F3] [[def-canonical-natural]] and [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]: write $\iota_{\mathbb N}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical natural map, with $\iota_{\mathbb N}(0)=0$ and $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))=\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)+1$. It is positive on positive naturals and strictly increases there. Thus the displayed denominator $n+1$ means $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))$, not a von Neumann set used as a real number.

[F4] [[lem-of-q-embeds]]: the rational embedding into $\mathbb R$ preserves order, so every rational $q>0$ has positive real image $\hat q$. [[cor-of-one-positive]], [[lem-of-inverse-positive]], and [[lem-of-sign-rules]] supply $1>0$, positivity of the inverse of a positive real, and reversal of order by reciprocation on positive reals.

[F5] [[def-real-limit]]: a real sequence converges to $0$ when, for every rational $q>0$, its absolute value is eventually less than $\hat q$.

## Proof

**Given:** [F1]–[F5].

1.1 The set $N_{\mathbb R}:=\{\iota_{\mathbb N}(n):n\in\mathbb N\}$ is nonempty. If it were bounded above, completeness [F1] would give $s=\sup N_{\mathbb R}$. Since $1>0$ by [F4], $s-1<s$, so $s-1$ is not an upper bound; choose $n\in\mathbb N$ with $\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)>s-1$. By the successor rule in [F3], $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))=\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)+1>s$, while $\sigma(n)\in\mathbb N$, contradicting that $s$ is an upper bound. Hence $N_{\mathbb R}$ is unbounded above. [F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 For every $n\in\mathbb N$, $\sigma(n)=1+n$ by natural-addition commutativity and the successor rule, so $1\le\sigma(n)$ by the definition of natural order; hence $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))>0$ by [F3]. The successor recursion gives $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(\sigma(n)))=\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))+1>\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))$, since $1>0$. Reciprocation reverses this strict inequality by [F4], hence $0<\epsilon_n$ and $\epsilon_{n+1}<\epsilon_n$. Now fix rational $q>0$ and let $\hat q>0$ be its real image. By step 1.1 choose $N\in\mathbb N$ with $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(N))>1/\hat q$. If $n\ge N$, then $\sigma(N)\le\sigma(n)$ by [F2] and [[lem-nat-order-add-compatible]], and the increasing-map clause of [F3] gives $\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))\ge\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(N))$. Therefore $0<\epsilon_n\le 1/\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(N))<\hat q$. This is convergence to zero by [F5]. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Under [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]], for compounds $A,B$ with $m(A)=m(B)$ and any compound $C$, $A+C\preceq B+C$ if and only if $A\preceq B$. The signed relation of [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] is well-defined; on nonnegative equal-mass maps it agrees with $\preceq$, is invariant under adding the same finite-support signed map to both sides, and is transitive and closed under adding two comparisons.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]]: compounds are finite-support nonnegative maps; their masses are finite sums, additive under composition and homogeneous under positive scaling.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]: $\preceq$ is a preorder, composition-consistent, positively scale-invariant, admits splitting/recombination, satisfies the stated positive-spectator stability axiom, and has CH.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]]: for equal-total finite signed maps $u,v$, the signed comparison is defined by comparing $(v-u)^-$ with $(v-u)^+$.

[F3] [[def-canonical-natural]] and [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] give the canonical embedding $\iota_{\mathbb N}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$, whose successor values are positive and are finite sums of $1$. [[lem-tdmath-reciprocal-naturals-tend-zero]] gives the real sequence $\epsilon_k=1/\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(k))>0$, $k\in\mathbb N$, with $\epsilon_k\to0$.

## Proof

**Given:** [F1], [A1], [F2], and [F3].

1.1 For equal-total $u,v$, $d=v-u$ has finite support and total sum zero. Pointwise $d=d^+-d^-$, so finite-sum linearity gives $m(d^+)-m(d^-)=0$; both maps are finite-support and nonnegative. Thus the definition in [F2] compares equal-mass compounds. If $u,v$ are nonnegative, set $k(x)=\min\{u(x),v(x)\}$; then $u=k+(v-u)^-$ and $v=k+(v-u)^+$. [F1, F2]

1.2 Suppose $A+C\preceq B+C$ and $m(C)>0$. For each $k\in\mathbb N$, set $n=\sigma(k)$ and $r=\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)>0$, and write $A/r=(1/r)A$. The embedding's successor rule and finite induction show that the sum of $n$ copies of $A/r$ is $r(A/r)=A$, and likewise for $B$. Scaling the given comparison by $1/r$ gives $A/r+C/r\preceq B/r+C/r$. By composition consistency, replace the $n$ copies of $A/r$ one at a time by $B/r$, keeping the already replaced copies, the remaining copies, and $C/r$ as spectators; after these finitely many replacements, $A+\epsilon_k C\preceq B+\epsilon_k C$. This holds for every natural index $k$. By [F3], $\epsilon_k>0$ and $\epsilon_k\to0$, so stability with $Z_0=Z_1=C$ gives $A\preceq B$. If $m(C)=0$, nonnegativity implies $C=0$ and the conclusion is the premise itself. Conversely, $A\preceq B$ gives $A+C\preceq B+C$ by consistency. [A1, F1, F3, algebra, induction]

2.1 For nonnegative $u,v$, step 1.1 gives $u=k+(v-u)^-$ and $v=k+(v-u)^+$. Cancellation from step 1.2 shows $u\preceq v$ exactly when $(v-u)^-\preceq(v-u)^+$, which is $u\preceq_s v$. For general signed maps, adding a common map leaves $v-u$ unchanged, so it leaves signed comparison unchanged. [F2, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 If $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s w$, consistency gives $N\preceq P$, where $N:=(v-u)^-+(w-v)^-$ and $P:=(v-u)^++(w-v)^+$. Pointwise $P-N=w-u$. Set $K(x):=\min\{P(x),N(x)\}$. If $P(x)\ge N(x)$ then $P(x)-K(x)=(w-u)^+(x)$ and $N(x)-K(x)=(w-u)^-(x)$; if $P(x)<N(x)$ the same identities follow with the two sides exchanged. Thus $P=K+(w-u)^+$ and $N=K+(w-u)^-$, with all four maps finite-support and nonnegative. Cancellation from step 1.2 gives $(w-u)^-\preceq(w-u)^+$, hence $u\preceq_s w$. For two independent signed comparisons, the same pointwise decomposition of the sums of their positive and negative parts proves closure under adding comparisons. Reflexivity follows because $0\preceq0$. [A1, F2, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $x_0,x_1\in X$ satisfy $x_0\preceq x_1$ and not $x_1\preceq x_0$. For every real $\lambda$, define the signed unit-mass reference map $R_\lambda:=(1-\lambda)e_{x_0}+\lambda e_{x_1}$. For all $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$,

$$R_\lambda\preceq_s R_\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda\le\mu.$$

The parameters need not lie in $[0,1]$; outside that interval $R_\lambda$ is signed notation, not a compound.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]: the relation is reflexive, positively scale-invariant, and the reference states have the stated one-way comparison.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]]: signed comparison is determined by the positive and negative parts of the coefficient difference.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]: on positive maps the signed relation agrees with the compound relation, and its definition is well-defined for equal-total signed maps.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [F1], and [F2].

1.1 Put $\delta:=\mu-\lambda$. The coefficient difference is $R_\mu-R_\lambda=\delta(e_{x_1}-e_{x_0})$ and has total zero. If $\delta>0$, its negative and positive parts are $\delta e_{x_0}$ and $\delta e_{x_1}$; if $\delta<0$, they are $(-\delta)e_{x_1}$ and $(-\delta)e_{x_0}$; if $\delta=0$, both are zero. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 If $\delta=0$, reflexivity gives $R_\lambda\preceq_sR_\mu$. If $\delta>0$, [F1] reduces this comparison to $\delta e_{x_0}\preceq\delta e_{x_1}$, which follows by positive scaling of $x_0\preceq x_1$ by $\delta$. Hence $\lambda<\mu$ implies $R_\lambda\preceq_sR_\mu$. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 If $\delta<0$ and $R_\lambda\preceq_sR_\mu$, [F1] gives $c e_{x_1}\preceq c e_{x_0}$ for $c:=-\delta>0$. In the ordered real field, $c^{-1}>0$: $c^{-1}\ne0$, and if $-c^{-1}>0$ then closure of the positive cone under multiplication gives $c(-c^{-1})=-1>0$. But $1>0$: since $1\ne0$, trichotomy gives either $1>0$ or $-1>0$; the latter would, by positive-product closure, also give $(-1)^2=1>0$, contradicting trichotomy. Thus $-1>0$ is impossible, and so $c^{-1}>0$. Positive scaling by $c^{-1}$ therefore implies $x_1\preceq x_0$, contrary to [A1]. Thus this comparison fails when $\lambda>\mu$. The three cases prove the equivalence. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] on compounds over a nonempty state set $X$, a strict reference pair $x_0\preceq x_1$ with not $x_1\preceq x_0$, and the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. For $x\in X$ define

$$L_x:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R:R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x\}.$$

Then $L_x$ is nonempty, bounded above, and downward closed. Its supremum $S(x):=\sup L_x$ is a real number and satisfies $R_{S(x)}\sim_s e_x$. Stability is used to prove attainment; no continuity of states or order is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]: equal-mass compounds form a preorder with consistency, positive scaling, stability for fixed positive spectators, and CH.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]]: $e_x$ has mass one, compound masses are finite sums, and composition/scaling preserve the stated masses.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] and [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]: signed comparisons are well-defined, translation-invariant, and agree with ordinary comparison on nonnegative compounds. For a finite-support signed map $u$, write $u^+(y):=\max\{u(y),0\}$ and $u^-(y):=\max\{-u(y),0\}$ pointwise; these are finite-support nonnegative maps with $u+u^-=u^+$, and this notation extends the positive and negative parts used in [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] to each signed reference map $R_\lambda$ itself.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-reference-order]]: $R_\lambda\preceq_sR_\mu$ exactly when $\lambda\le\mu$.

[F4] [[lem-tdmath-reciprocal-naturals-tend-zero]]: for $n\in\mathbb N$, $\epsilon_n:=1/q_n$ with $q_n:=\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))$ is positive, strictly decreasing, and converges to zero. Its canonical-natural convention gives $\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)\ge0$ and $q_n=\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)+1\ge1$; natural indices and their real images are distinguished.

[F5] [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: every nonempty bounded-above subset of $\mathbb R$ has a supremum.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1]–[F5], with $x\in X$ fixed.

1.1 Write $q_n:=\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(n))>0$, so $\epsilon_n=1/q_n$ by [F4]. Suppose no $n\in\mathbb N$ satisfies $(q_n+1)e_{x_0}\preceq q_ne_{x_1}+e_x$. Both sides have mass $q_n+1$, so CH gives $q_ne_{x_1}+e_x\preceq(q_n+1)e_{x_0}$. Scale by $1/q_n=\epsilon_n$ to obtain $e_{x_1}+\epsilon_ne_x\preceq e_{x_0}+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}$. Apply stability to the sequence $\epsilon_n$, with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and positive unit-mass spectators $e_x,e_{x_0}$. It yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, contradicting strictness. Thus some $n$ has $(q_n+1)e_{x_0}\preceq q_ne_{x_1}+e_x$, which by signed translation and cancellation in [F2] is $R_{-q_n}\preceq_s e_x$; hence $-q_n\in L_x$. [A1, F1, F2, F4]

1.2 Suppose $L_x$ is unbounded above. For each $n\in\mathbb N$, unboundedness supplies $\lambda\in L_x$ with $\lambda>q_n$; [F3] gives $R_{q_n}\preceq_sR_\lambda$, and transitivity gives $q_n\in L_x$. Since $q_n\ge1$ by [F4], adding the common compound $q_ne_{x_0}$ to $R_{q_n}$ and $e_x$ makes them $e_{x_0}+q_ne_{x_1}$ and $e_x+q_ne_{x_0}$. Thus [F2] identifies $R_{q_n}\preceq_s e_x$ with the compound comparison between those maps. Scaling by $\epsilon_n=1/q_n$ gives $e_{x_1}+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}\preceq e_{x_0}+\epsilon_ne_x$. Stability with bases $e_{x_1},e_{x_0}$ and positive unit-mass spectators $e_{x_0},e_x$ now yields $x_1\preceq x_0$, again a contradiction. Therefore $L_x$ is bounded above. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4]

2.1 If $\lambda\in L_x$ and $\mu\le\lambda$, [F3] gives $R_\mu\preceq_sR_\lambda$; signed transitivity and $R_\lambda\preceq_s e_x$ imply $\mu\in L_x$. Thus $L_x$ is downward closed. By steps 1.1 and 1.2 it is nonempty and bounded above, so [F5] supplies the real number $s:=\sup L_x$. [A1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 For each $n\in\mathbb N$, $s-\epsilon_n$ is not an upper bound of $L_x$, so some $\lambda\in L_x$ has $\lambda>s-\epsilon_n$. Downward closure gives $s-\epsilon_n\in L_x$. Consistency then gives $R_s+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}\preceq_s e_x+\epsilon_ne_{x_1}$, because $R_{s-\epsilon_n}+\epsilon_ne_{x_1}=R_s+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}$. Let $K:=R_s^-$. Adding the fixed nonnegative map $K$ to both sides converts this signed comparison into the compound comparison $R_s^++\epsilon_ne_{x_0}\preceq e_x+K+\epsilon_ne_{x_1}$. Their bases have equal mass because $m(R_s^+)-m(K)=1=m(e_x)$. Stability with positive unit-mass spectators $e_{x_0},e_{x_1}$ yields $R_s^+\preceq e_x+K$, that is, $R_s\preceq_s e_x$. [A1, F1, F2, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 Since $s$ is an upper bound, $s+\epsilon_n\notin L_x$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. To derive the reverse signed comparison from CH, set $H_n:=R_{s+\epsilon_n}^-$. The translated maps $e_x+H_n$ and $R_{s+\epsilon_n}+H_n=R_{s+\epsilon_n}^+$ are nonnegative compounds. Since $R_{s+\epsilon_n}=R_{s+\epsilon_n}^+-H_n$ has total coefficient one, finite-sum linearity gives $m(R_{s+\epsilon_n}^+)-m(H_n)=1$; with $m(e_x)=1$, the translated compounds have equal mass $1+m(H_n)$. CH applies to this pair. If it gave $R_{s+\epsilon_n}^+\preceq e_x+H_n$, signed translation invariance in [F2] would imply $R_{s+\epsilon_n}\preceq_s e_x$, contrary to $s+\epsilon_n\notin L_x$. Therefore it gives $e_x+H_n\preceq R_{s+\epsilon_n}^+$, which by [F2] is $e_x\preceq_s R_{s+\epsilon_n}$. Add $\epsilon_ne_{x_0}$ to both signed maps and use $R_{s+\epsilon_n}+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}=R_s+\epsilon_ne_{x_1}$. Then add $K=R_s^-$ to both; the resulting equal-mass compound comparison is $e_x+K+\epsilon_ne_{x_0}\preceq R_s^++\epsilon_ne_{x_1}$. Stability with bases $e_x+K,R_s^+$ and positive unit-mass spectators $e_{x_0},e_{x_1}$ gives $e_x+K\preceq R_s^+$, or $e_x\preceq_sR_s$. Together with step 3.1 this proves $R_s\sim_s e_x$ and the claimed attainment. [A1, F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $X$ be nonempty and suppose its finite-support compounds carry the comparison structure of [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]] over the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$. If there are $x_0,x_1\in X$ with $x_0\preceq x_1$ and not $x_1\preceq x_0$, define $S(x):=\sup L_x$ using [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]]. Then $S:X\to\mathbb R$ is normalized by $S(x_0)=0$, $S(x_1)=1$, and for all equal-mass compounds $A=\sum_i a_i e_{x_i}$ and $B=\sum_j b_j e_{y_j}$,

$$A\preceq B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_i a_iS(x_i)\le\sum_j b_jS(y_j).$$

Thus $S$ is an additive extensive representation on finite compounds. If no strict pair exists, CH instead makes every equal-mass pair of compounds equivalent, and any constant state function gives a (degenerate) additive representation. No concavity, continuity, or physical law follows without additional hypotheses.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] [[def-tdmath-comparison-and-stability]]: equal-mass compounds satisfy the preorder, consistency, scaling, stability and comparison hypotheses; the state set is nonempty.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-signed-comparison]] and [[lem-tdmath-spectator-cancellation]]: signed comparisons are translation-invariant and additive, and agree with ordinary comparison for nonnegative compounds.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-reference-supremum-bounds]]: in the strict-reference case, each $S(x)=\sup L_x$ is finite and $x\sim_sR_{S(x)}$.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-reference-order]]: $R_\lambda\preceq_sR_\mu$ iff $\lambda\le\mu$ for the chosen strict reference pair.

[F4] [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] and [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]]: each state denotes its unit-mass point compound $e_x$; every compound is the finite sum of its strictly positive support coefficients, or the empty sum. Nonnegative scaling is pointwise, $0C=0$, and a nonnegative compound has zero mass exactly when it is empty.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1] and [F1]–[F4].

1.1 In the strict-reference case, [F3] gives $R_\lambda\preceq_s e_{x_0}$ exactly for $\lambda\le0$, and $R_\lambda\preceq_s e_{x_1}$ exactly for $\lambda\le1$. Their suprema are therefore $S(x_0)=0$ and $S(x_1)=1$. [F2, F3]

1.2 Let $C=\sum_i a_i e_{x_i}$ have mass $M$ and set $q_C:=\sum_i a_iS(x_i)$. Discard any zero terms in this presentation using [F4]. If the support is empty, $C=0$, $M=q_C=0$ and $C_R=0$, so signed reflexivity gives the claimed equivalence. Otherwise each remaining coefficient is strictly positive. For each remaining constituent, [F2] gives $e_{x_i}\sim_sR_{S(x_i)}$; positive scaling and finite repeated use of composition combine these into $C\sim_s C_R$, where $C_R:=\sum_i a_iR_{S(x_i)}=(M-q_C)e_{x_0}+q_Ce_{x_1}$. This calculation is valid for signed coefficients because the signed relation is additive and translation-invariant by [F1]. [A1, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 Apply step 1.2 to both $A$ and $B$, and write $q_A,q_B$ for the resulting scalar sums. Since $A\sim_sA_R$ and $B\sim_sB_R$, transitivity gives $A\preceq B$ exactly when $A_R\preceq_sB_R$. Their masses agree, and $B_R-A_R=(q_B-q_A)(e_{x_1}-e_{x_0})$; [F3] therefore gives $A_R\preceq_sB_R$ exactly when $q_A\le q_B$. This proves the representation formula. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.2]

3.1 In the no-strict-pair case, take any $x,y\in X$. By [F4] their unit compounds have equal mass one, so CH gives one of $x\preceq y$ or $y\preceq x$; if exactly one held it would be a strict pair, so both hold. Fix $r\in X$. Let $C$ have mass $M$. If $M=0$, [F4] gives $C=0$, and reflexivity handles this empty compound without applying the positive-scaling axiom at zero. If $M>0$, use the canonical finite decomposition over the support from [F4]; every coefficient there is positive. Scale each constituent equivalence $e_x\sim e_r$ by its positive coefficient and compose the finitely many comparisons to obtain $C\sim M e_r$. Thus equal-mass $A,B$ are both empty when their common mass is zero, and otherwise each is equivalent to the same $M e_r$; hence they are equivalent in both cases. For a constant $S(x)=c$, both compound values equal $cM$, including zero for empty compounds, so the representation equivalence holds. [A1, F1, F4, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. Write $\overline{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ with its usual order and extended addition; in a convex combination set $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ and $\lambda\cdot(+\infty)=+\infty$ for $\lambda>0$. A function $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **proper** when it never takes the value $-\infty$ and its effective domain

$$\operatorname{dom}f:=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:f(x)<+\infty\}$$

is nonempty. It is **convex** when

$$f((1-t)x+ty)\le (1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d,\ t\in[0,1]).$$

It is **lower semicontinuous** when each weak sublevel set $\{x:f(x)\le a\}$ is closed in the Euclidean topology, for every $a\in\mathbb R$. Its **epigraph** is

$$\operatorname{epi}f:=\{(x,r)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R:f(x)\le r\}.$$

On this page “closed proper convex” means proper, convex, and lower semicontinuous in these conventions. The pairing of $p,x\in\mathbb R^d$ is the Euclidean inner product $\langle p,x\rangle$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

## Definition

Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be proper in the sense of [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]. Its **Fenchel conjugate** is $f^*:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,

$$f^*(p):=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}\bigl(\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)\bigr).$$

The supremum is taken in $\overline{\mathbb R}$; its defining set is nonempty and consists of real numbers, so $f^*(p)\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. The **biconjugate** is an extended-real expression that may also take $-\infty$ when its defining supremum is over the empty set:

$$f^{**}(x):=\sup_{\{p\in\mathbb R^d:f^*(p)<+\infty\}}\bigl(\langle p,x\rangle-f^*(p)\bigr),$$

with the convention $\sup\varnothing=-\infty$. For $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, the **subdifferential** is

$$\partial f(x):=\{p\in\mathbb R^d:f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle p,y-x\rangle\text{ for every }y\in\mathbb R^d\};$$

set $\partial f(x)=\varnothing$ for $x\notin\operatorname{dom}f$. A vector in $\partial f(x)$ is a subgradient at $x$. All pairings use [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ use the conventions of [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]. Then $f$ is convex if and only if $\operatorname{epi}f$ is a convex subset of $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, and $f$ is lower semicontinuous if and only if $\operatorname{epi}f$ is closed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $d\ge1$, the extended-real conventions and epigraph of the Statement, and the Euclidean topology.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]: convexity is the extended chord inequality; lower semicontinuity means that every weak sublevel set is closed.

[F2] [[def-metric-topology]]: a set is open when every point has a positive-radius metric ball contained in the set; it is closed exactly when its complement is open. Here the metrics are Euclidean.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Suppose $f$ is convex and take $(x,r),(y,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f$. For $t\in[0,1]$, the chord inequality gives $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\le(1-t)r+ts$, so $(1-t)(x,r)+t(y,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f$. Thus the epigraph is convex. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Conversely, if the epigraph is convex and $f(x),f(y)$ are finite, then $(x,f(x))$ and $(y,f(y))$ lie in it; their convex combination lies in it and gives the chord inequality. If either value is $+\infty$ and its coefficient is positive, the right side is $+\infty$ and the inequality is automatic; at $t=0$ or $t=1$ it is equality. [F1, algebra]

1.3 Suppose $\operatorname{epi}f$ is closed and fix $a\in\mathbb R$. For $n=d,d+1$ write $d_n(u,v)=\bigl(\sum_{j=1}^n(u_j-v_j)^2\bigr)^{1/2}$ for the Euclidean metric. The slice map $i_a(x)=(x,a)$ satisfies $d_{d+1}(i_a(x),i_a(y))=d_d(x,y)$. If $f(x)>a$, then $(x,a)\notin\operatorname{epi}f$; closedness gives $\varepsilon>0$ such that the $d_{d+1}$-ball of radius $\varepsilon$ around $(x,a)$ misses $\operatorname{epi}f$. Whenever $d_d(x,y)<\varepsilon$, the distance identity puts $(y,a)$ in that ball, so $f(y)>a$. Thus the complement of $\{y:f(y)\le a\}$ is open, and this weak sublevel set is closed. [F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Conversely suppose every weak sublevel set is closed and let $(x,r)\notin\operatorname{epi}f$, so $r<f(x)$. Choose a finite real $a$ with $r<a<f(x)$ when $f(x)$ is finite, and choose $a=r+1$ when $f(x)=+\infty$. The set $N=\{y:f(y)>a\}$ is an open neighborhood of $x$, as it is the complement of a closed weak sublevel set. Choose $\delta>0$ with $B_d(x,\delta)\subseteq N$ and $\eta>0$ with $r+\eta<a$. If $d_{d+1}((x,r),(y,s))<\min(\delta,\eta)$, then $y\in N$ and $s<r+\eta<a<f(y)$, so $(y,s)\notin\operatorname{epi}f$. The epigraph's complement therefore contains a ball around each of its points and is open, so the epigraph is closed. [given, F1, F2, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be proper, let $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, and let $p\in\mathbb R^d$. Then $f^*(p)\ge\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)$. Equality holds exactly when $p\in\partial f(x)$, equivalently when $x$ attains the supremum defining $f^*(p)$; in that case the supremum is finite.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Fenchel conjugate and subdifferential from [[def-tdmath-fenchel-transform-and-subgradient]].

[F1] [[def-tdmath-fenchel-transform-and-subgradient]]: $f^*(p)$ is the supremum of $\langle p,y\rangle-f(y)$ over $y\in\operatorname{dom}f$, and $p\in\partial f(x)$ means $f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle p,y-x\rangle$ for every $y$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Since $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, the value $\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)$ is one of the values over which $f^*(p)$ is the supremum; the stated inequality follows. [F1, given]

2.1 Equality means every $y\in\operatorname{dom}f$ satisfies $\langle p,y\rangle-f(y)\le\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)$, which rearranges to the subgradient inequality; for $y\notin\operatorname{dom}f$ that inequality is automatic because $f(y)=+\infty$. Conversely the subgradient inequalities make the value at $x$ a finite upper bound attained there, so $f^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)$. [F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $z\notin E$. Then there are a nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^n$ and a real $c$ such that

$$\langle u,e\rangle\le c<\langle u,z\rangle\qquad(e\in E).$$

Thus an affine hyperplane strictly separates the point from the entire set.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Euclidean inner product and norm, a nonempty closed convex $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and $z\notin E$.

[F1] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: $\|x\|_2^2=\langle x,x\rangle$ and the squared norm expands bilinearly.

[F2] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: for $e_0,e_1\in E$ and $t\in[0,1]$, $(1-t)e_0+te_1\in E$.

[L1] [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: the Euclidean norm satisfies the triangle inequality, so $e\mapsto\|z-e\|_2$ is continuous by the reverse triangle inequality.

[L2] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: a closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, is compact.

[L3] [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]: a continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact metric space attains its minimum.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Choose $e_0\in E$ and set $R=\|z-e_0\|_2+1$. The set $K=E\cap\{e:\|z-e\|_2\le R\}$ is nonempty and bounded; it is closed because $E$ is closed and the distance map is continuous by [L1]. Hence [L2] makes it compact, and the continuous function $e\mapsto\|z-e\|_2^2$ attains a minimum at some $e_*\in K$ by [L3]. [given, L1, L2, L3, choose]

2.1 This $e_*$ is nearest to $z$ in all of $E$: every $e\in E\setminus K$ satisfies $\|z-e\|_2>R>\|z-e_0\|_2\ge\|z-e_*\|_2$. Put $u=z-e_*$; since $z\notin E$, $u\ne0$. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Fix $e\in E$ and put $v=e-e_*$. For $0<t\le1$, [F2] gives $e_*+tv\in E$, so minimality of $e_*$ and [F1] imply $2t\langle u,v\rangle\le t^2\|v\|_2^2$. If $\langle u,v\rangle>0$, then $v\ne0$; setting $t=\min\{1,\langle u,v\rangle/\|v\|_2^2\}$ contradicts this inequality whether the minimum is $1$ or the quotient. Hence $\langle u,v\rangle\le0$. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Therefore $\langle u,e\rangle\le\langle u,e_*\rangle$ for every $e\in E$, while $\langle u,z\rangle=\langle u,e_*\rangle+\|u\|_2^2>\langle u,e_*\rangle$. Taking $c=\langle u,e_*\rangle$ proves strict separation. [F1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be closed, proper, and convex in the sense of [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]. With the Fenchel conjugate and biconjugate of [[def-tdmath-fenchel-transform-and-subgradient]], one has

$$f^{**}(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^d).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The closed proper convex function and conjugates in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]]: proper means $\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing$ and $f>-\infty$; convexity is the extended chord inequality; lower semicontinuity means closed weak sublevel sets.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-extended-convex-epigraph-equivalence]]: under [F1], $\operatorname{epi}f$ is nonempty, closed, and convex.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-closed-convex-separation]]: a point outside a nonempty closed convex subset of $\mathbb R^{d+1}$ has a strict linear separator.

[F4] [[def-tdmath-fenchel-transform-and-subgradient]]: $f^*(p)$ and $f^{**}(x)$ are the stated extended suprema over the effective domain and finite conjugate domain.

[L1] [[thm-of-archimedean]]: the canonical natural numbers are cofinal in $\mathbb R$; for every $q\in\mathbb R$ there is a positive integer $k$ with $q<k$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For any $x$ with $f(x)<+\infty$ and any $p$ with $f^*(p)<+\infty$, the defining supremum gives $f^*(p)\ge\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)$, hence $\langle p,x\rangle-f^*(p)\le f(x)$; taking the supremum over $p$ yields $f^{**}(x)\le f(x)$. If $f(x)=+\infty$, the same upper bound is automatic. [F4, given, algebra]

1.2 Fix $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$ and a real $t<f(x)$. Apply [F3] to $(x,t)$ and the nonempty closed convex set $\operatorname{epi}f$, and negate the resulting separator to write $\langle a,y\rangle+bs\ge c>\langle a,x\rangle+bt$ for all $(y,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f$. Upward closure forces $b\ge0$. If $b=0$, the inequality at $(x,f(x))\in\operatorname{epi}f$ would give $\langle a,x\rangle\ge c>\langle a,x\rangle$, impossible. Thus $b>0$. [F2, F3, given, algebra]

1.3 Now fix $x\notin\operatorname{dom}f$ and $t\in\mathbb R$. Apply [F3] to $(x,t)$ and negate the separator to obtain $\langle a,y\rangle+bs\ge c>\langle a,x\rangle+bt$ for all $(y,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f$. If $b>0$, then $f(y)\ge-\langle a/b,y\rangle+c/b$ for every $y\in\operatorname{dom}f$, so with $p=-a/b$ one has $f^*(p)\le-c/b<+\infty$ and $f^{**}(x)\ge\langle p,x\rangle-f^*(p)\ge(c-\langle a,x\rangle)/b>t$. [F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Substituting $(y,f(y))$ for every $y\in\operatorname{dom}f$ gives the affine minorant $\ell(y)=-\langle a/b,y\rangle+c/b\le f(y)$. With $p=-a/b$, [F4] gives $f^*(p)\le-c/b$, hence $f^{**}(x)\ge\langle p,x\rangle-f^*(p)\ge\ell(x)>t$. Since this holds for every $t<f(x)$, $f^{**}(x)\ge f(x)$ on $\operatorname{dom}f$. [F4, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 In the $b=0$ case of step 1.3, the separator gives $\langle a,y\rangle\ge c>\langle a,x\rangle$ for every $y\in\operatorname{dom}f$. Choose $y_0\in\operatorname{dom}f$ and a finite $t_0<f(y_0)$. Apply [F3] to $(y_0,t_0)$ and $\operatorname{epi}f$, reversing the separator orientation to obtain $\langle a_0,y\rangle+b_0s\ge c_0>\langle a_0,y_0\rangle+b_0t_0$ for every $(y,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f$. Upward closure gives $b_0\ge0$, and $b_0=0$ contradicts the inequality at $(y_0,f(y_0))$, so $b_0>0$. Set $p_0=-a_0/b_0$ and $r_0=c_0/b_0$; substituting $(y,f(y))$ gives the affine minorant $\ell_0(y)=\langle p_0,y\rangle+r_0\le f(y)$ on $\operatorname{dom}f$, so [F4] gives $f^*(p_0)\le-r_0$. For each positive integer $k$, define $\ell_k(y)=\ell_0(y)+k(c-\langle a,y\rangle)=\langle p_0-ka,y\rangle+(r_0+kc)$. Since $c-\langle a,y\rangle\le0$ on $\operatorname{dom}f$, this is still a minorant; [F4] gives $f^*(p_0-ka)\le-(r_0+kc)<+\infty$ and hence $f^{**}(x)\ge\ell_k(x)=\ell_0(x)+k\delta$, where $\delta:=c-\langle a,x\rangle>0$ by step 1.3. For any prescribed $B\in\mathbb R$, apply [L1] to $q=(B-\ell_0(x))/\delta$ to choose a positive integer $k$ with $q<k$; multiplying by $\delta>0$ gives $\ell_0(x)+k\delta>B$. Hence $f^{**}(x)$ exceeds every real bound, so $f^{**}(x)=+\infty=f(x)$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, L1, step 1.3, choose, algebra]

3.1 The upper bound from step 1.1 and the lower bounds from steps 2.1 and 2.2 cover respectively finite and infinite values of $f(x)$, proving equality everywhere. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

## Statement

Let $m\ge1$ and $d\ge1$ be integers, let $q_1,\ldots,q_m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$. Put

$$\Delta_m=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^m:\theta_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i=1\},\qquad P:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_iq_i:\theta\in\Delta_m\right\}.$$

Thus $P$ is the finite convex hull of the listed points, defined here as their convex combinations.

For $x\in P$ let $\Theta_x=\{\theta\in\Delta_m:\sum_i\theta_iq_i=x\}$ and define

$$f_{\rm mix}(x)=\min_{\theta\in\Theta_x}\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i a_i;$$

set $f_{\rm mix}(x)=+\infty$ for $x\notin P$. Then every minimum is attained; $f_{\rm mix}$ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex; and it is pointwise greatest among convex functions $h:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ satisfying $h(q_i)\le a_i$ for every $i$. Consequently $f_{\rm mix}=f_{\rm mix}^{**}$. If $p\in\partial f_{\rm mix}(x)$ and $\theta$ is any minimizing mixture for $x$, then every $i$ with $\theta_i>0$ satisfies

$$a_i=\langle p,q_i\rangle-f_{\rm mix}^*(p).$$

Thus all occupied data points $(q_i,a_i)$ lie on one supporting affine hyperplane. The assertion is finite-dimensional and makes no claim about infinite families.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite data in the Statement, the extended-real conventions of [[def-tdmath-extended-convex-function]], and the conjugate and subgradient definitions of [[def-tdmath-fenchel-transform-and-subgradient]].

[F1] The set $\Delta_m$ is nonempty, closed, and bounded: it contains each coordinate vector; it is the intersection of the closed coordinate half-spaces $\{\theta_i\ge0\}$ with the closed affine set $\{\sum_i\theta_i=1\}$; and every coordinate satisfies $0\le\theta_i\le1$, so $\|\theta\|_2^2=\sum_i\theta_i^2\le m$. Hence [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] makes it compact. The map $Q(\theta)=\sum_i\theta_iq_i$ is linear and continuous by [L1], so $\Theta_x=\Delta_m\cap Q^{-1}(\{x\})$ is closed and bounded, hence compact. The objective $\theta\mapsto\sum_i\theta_i a_i$ is also linear and continuous by [L1].

[F2] A continuous image of a compact metric space is compact ([[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]).

[F3] A continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space attains its minimum ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

[F4] The epigraph characterizations of extended convexity and lower semicontinuity are [[lem-tdmath-extended-convex-epigraph-equivalence]].

[F5] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: a convex set contains every segment between two of its points.

[F6] A closed proper convex function equals its biconjugate ([[thm-tdmath-finite-dimensional-biconjugation]]).

[F7] Equality in Fenchel's inequality is equivalent to the subgradient relation ([[lem-tdmath-fenchel-young-equality]]).

[L1] [[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]: every linear map between finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces is continuous.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The set $\Delta_m$ contains each coordinate vector. The coordinate maps, the sum map $\theta\mapsto\sum_i\theta_i$, and $Q$ are continuous by [L1]. For any continuous map $T$ into a Euclidean space and any closed set $K$, the complement of $T^{-1}(K)$ is open: if $T(z)\notin K$, a ball about $T(z)$ misses $K$, and continuity gives a ball about $z$ mapped inside that ball. Thus $T^{-1}(K)$ is closed. Coordinate half-lines $[0,\infty)$ and singletons are closed, since a point outside either has a positive-distance ball missing it; a finite intersection of closed sets is closed because its complement is a finite union of open sets. These facts show that $\Delta_m$ is closed and that $\Theta_x=\Delta_m\cap Q^{-1}(\{x\})$ is closed. Since $0\le\theta_i\le1$ on $\Delta_m$, both sets are bounded and hence compact by [F1]. For $x\in P$, the definition of $P$ makes $\Theta_x$ nonempty. The linear objective is continuous by [L1] and attains its minimum on $\Theta_x$ by [F3]. [F1, F3, L1, given, construct]

2.1 Let $C=\{\sum_i\theta_i(q_i,a_i):\theta\in\Delta_m\}\subset\mathbb R^{d+1}$ and $V=\{(0,s):s\ge0\}$. The affine map defining $C$ is continuous by [L1], so $C$ is compact by [F2]. The set $C$ is convex because convex combinations of points in $\Delta_m$ remain in $\Delta_m$ (nonnegativity and the unit-sum equation are preserved) and the defining map is affine; $V$ is closed and convex. If $(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f_{\rm mix}$, a minimizing $\theta\in\Theta_x$ gives $(x,f_{\rm mix}(x))\in C$ and $r-f_{\rm mix}(x)\ge0$, so $(x,r)\in C+V$. Conversely if $(x,r)=\sum_i\theta_i(q_i,a_i)+(0,s)$ with $s\ge0$, then $f_{\rm mix}(x)\le\sum_i\theta_i a_i\le r$. Thus $\operatorname{epi}f_{\rm mix}=C+V$. [F1, F2, L1, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 The coordinate vector with $\theta_i=1$ and all other weights zero shows $f_{\rm mix}(q_i)\le a_i$. Let $h:\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be convex with $h(q_i)\le a_i$. For any weights $\theta\in\Delta_m$, prove $h(\sum_i\theta_iq_i)\le\sum_i\theta_i h(q_i)$ by induction on the number $N$ of positive weights: for $N=1$ it is equality; for $N>1$, choose an index $j$ with $0<\theta_j<1$, put $y=(1-\theta_j)^{-1}\sum_{i\ne j}\theta_iq_i$, and apply the induction hypothesis to the normalized remaining weights. Convexity then gives $h(\sum_i\theta_iq_i)\le\theta_jh(q_j)+(1-\theta_j)h(y)\le\sum_i\theta_i h(q_i)$. All terms on the right are finite because $h(q_i)\le a_i$ and the codomain excludes $-\infty$. For $x\in P$ and any $\theta\in\Theta_x$, this gives $h(x)\le\sum_i\theta_i a_i$; taking the minimum yields $h(x)\le f_{\rm mix}(x)$. For $x\notin P$, $h(x)\le+\infty=f_{\rm mix}(x)$. Thus $f_{\rm mix}$ is the greatest convex minorant of the data. [F4, given, step 1.1, algebra, induction]

3.1 The set $C+V$ is convex: for $c_1,c_2\in C$, $v_1,v_2\in V$, and $t\in[0,1]$, $(1-t)(c_1+v_1)+t(c_2+v_2)=((1-t)c_1+tc_2)+((1-t)v_1+tv_2)\in C+V$ by [F5]. To see it is closed, fix $z=(x,r)\notin C+V$ and write $c=(u,a)\in C$. The distance from $z$ to the ray $c+V$ is $\rho_z(c)=\sqrt{\|x-u\|_2^2+\max\{a-r,0\}^2}$: if $r\ge a$ the closest ray point has height $r$, and if $r<a$ it has height $a$. This formula is continuous in $c$ because $\max\{w,0\}=(w+|w|)/2$, and it is positive for every $c\in C$ since $z\notin c+V$. Compactness of $C$ and [F3] give a minimum $\delta>0$; every point of $C+V$ is at distance at least $\delta$ from $z$, so the ball of radius $\delta/2$ about $z$ misses $C+V$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F4] and step 3.1, $f_{\rm mix}$ is convex and lower semicontinuous. It is proper because $P$ is nonempty, each value on $P$ is finite by step 1.1, and it is $+\infty$ outside $P$. Therefore [F6] gives $f_{\rm mix}=f_{\rm mix}^{**}$. [F4, F6, step 1.1, step 3.1]

5.1 Let $p\in\partial f_{\rm mix}(x)$ and let $\theta$ attain the minimum defining $f_{\rm mix}(x)$. By [F7], $f_{\rm mix}^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle-f_{\rm mix}(x)$. Also $f_{\rm mix}(q_i)\le a_i$ implies $\langle p,q_i\rangle-a_i\le\langle p,q_i\rangle-f_{\rm mix}(q_i)\le f_{\rm mix}^*(p)$. Since $\langle p,x\rangle-f_{\rm mix}(x)=\sum_i\theta_i(\langle p,q_i\rangle-a_i)$ is a weighted average of terms bounded above by $f_{\rm mix}^*(p)$, each term with $\theta_i>0$ equals that bound, proving the supporting-hyperplane formula. [F7, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

is concatenation of tensor factors, extended bilinearly, and its unit is $1$
in degree zero. Its conjugate-linear involution is specified on elementary
tensors by
$$(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)^*:=\overline{f_n}\otimes\cdots\otimes\overline{f_1},\qquad (c1)^*=\overline c1.$$

For $f_j\in S$, the elementary tensor is evaluated against a distribution by
the test function
$$J_n(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)(x_1,\ldots,x_n):=\prod_{j=1}^n f_j(x_j).$$
This is in $S_n$: for multi-indices split into four-coordinate blocks
$(\alpha_j,\beta_j)$, its Schwartz seminorm is
$$p_{(\alpha_j)_j,(\beta_j)_j}(J_n(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n))=\prod_{j=1}^n p_{\alpha_j\beta_j}(f_j).$$
Thus $J_n$ is multilinear and continuous, and the displayed formula extends
linearly to the algebraic tensor product.
In degree zero set $J_0(c1):=c$.

By these definitions concatenation is associative with the degree-zero unit,
and reversal together with complex conjugation is an involution satisfying
$(ab)^*=b^*a^*$; thus $T(S)$ is a unital complex star algebra.

A **positive tempered moment family** is a sequence consisting of $W_0=1$
and $W_n\in S_n'$ for each $n\ge1$ such that the multilinear maps
$$f_1,\ldots,f_n\longmapsto\langle W_n,J_n(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)\rangle$$
extend, degree by degree and then over finite sums, to a complex-linear
functional $\omega:T(S)\to\mathbb C$ satisfying
$$\omega(1)=1,\qquad \omega(a^*a)\in[0,\infty)\quad(a\in T(S)).$$
Equivalently, the family supplies an actually positive normalized functional
on this algebra. Positivity is a hypothesis on the distributions; formal
coefficient families do not qualify merely because they obey algebraic
identities. No topology on $T(S)$, norm completion, C*-algebra, or existence
claim for an interacting field is part of this definition.

## Statement

Let $x:I\to M$ be a $C^2$ future timelike curve on a nonempty open interval $I$, with parameter $s$ and tangent $T=dx/ds$. Fix $c>0$, $s_0\in I$, and $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$, and define $\ell(s)=\sqrt{-g(T,T)}$ and $\tau(s)=\tau_0+c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^s\ell(r)\,dr$. Then $\tau'(s)=\ell(s)/c>0$, so $\tau$ is an increasing $C^2$ coordinate on its open image $J=\tau(I)$. The tangent with respect to this parameter is $U=dx/d\tau=cT/\ell$ and satisfies $g(U,U)=-c^2$. This is a mathematical reparametrization result; by itself it does not identify $\tau$ with a physical clock reading.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A $C^2$ future timelike curve and the definitions in the Statement.

[F1] For a future timelike worldline, the proper-time density is $h=\sqrt{-g(T,T)}>0$ and its integral defines proper time ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]).

[F2] The fundamental theorem gives the derivative of an integral of a continuous density ([[thm-ftc-first-part]]); a $C^1$ map with nonzero derivative has a local $C^1$ inverse ([[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]]).

[F3] The chain rule gives $(x\circ\tau^{-1})'=T/(\tau')$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[F4] The mean value theorem applies on every compact subinterval of $I$ ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

By [F1] and [F2], $\tau$ is differentiable with $\tau'=\ell/c>0$. By [F4], the mean value theorem on each compact subinterval makes $\tau$ strictly increasing. [given, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 At each point the nonzero derivative gives a local inverse; injectivity makes those local inverses agree, so they define a $C^1$ inverse on the open image $J$. By [F3], $U=T/\tau'=cT/\ell$, and hence $g(U,U)=c^2g(T,T)/\ell^2=-c^2$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold, $a<b$, and $x:[a,b]\to M$ a $C^2$ future timelike curve. Put $T=dx/ds$, $\ell=\sqrt{-g(T,T)}>0$, and for a constant $m>0$ and $c>0$ define the length action $S[x]=-mc\int_a^b\ell(s)\,ds$. Let $H(\epsilon,s)$ be a $C^2$ fixed-endpoint variation through future timelike curves for $\epsilon$ near $0$, with $H(0,s)=x(s)$, $H(\epsilon,a)=x(a)$, $H(\epsilon,b)=x(b)$, and variation field $J=\partial_\epsilon H|_0$. Then

$$\delta S=\left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}S[H(\epsilon,\cdot)]\right|_{0}=-mc\int_a^b g\!\left(J,D_s\!\left(\frac{T}{\ell}\right)\right)ds.$$

Consequently $x$ is stationary under all such variations exactly when $D_s(T/\ell)=0$, equivalently $D_\tau U=0$ for the proper-time parameter of [[thm-rpm-proper-time-parametrization]]. The length integral has the same value under every orientation-preserving $C^1$ change of variable $s=\phi(r)$ with $\phi:[a',b']\to[a,b]$ a diffeomorphism and $\phi'>0$, namely $\int_{a'}^{b'}\ell_r(r)\,dr=\int_a^b\ell(s)\,ds$ for $T_r(r)=\phi'(r)T(\phi(r))$ and $\ell_r(r)=\sqrt{-g(T_r(r),T_r(r))}$. As a transformation of the stated $C^2$ curve and variation class, require instead that $\phi$ be an orientation-preserving $C^2$ diffeomorphism; then the stationarity equation is covariant, since $D_r(T_r/\ell_r)(r)=\phi'(r)(D_s(T/\ell))(\phi(r))$. This is a local variational statement; it makes no claim about global proper-time maximality, and the square-root action is not defined for a nonzero null tangent.

[F4] A smooth bump can be chosen equal to $1$ near an interior point and supported in a prescribed larger interval ([[lem-smooth-bump-between-concentric-euclidean-balls]]).

[F6] For a $C^2$ two-parameter map, mixed partial derivatives commute ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]).

[F7] A monotone $C^1$ change of parameter transforms the Riemann integral by its derivative ([[thm-monotone-change-of-variable-for-riemann-integrals]]).

[F9] In a chart, metric compatibility gives $\partial_bg_{ac}=\Gamma^d{}_{ba}g_{dc}+\Gamma^d{}_{bc}g_{ad}$, and torsion-freeness is equivalent to $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\Gamma^a{}_{cb}$ ([[lem-gr-connection-conditions-in-chart-components]]).

## Postulate

**Adopted convention.** On a prescribed background $(M,g,N)$ from [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]], let $x:[a,b]\to M$, $a<b$, be a continuous piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike curve in the sense of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]: it has a finite partition $a=s_0<\cdots<s_k=b$, each segment is $C^1$ up to its endpoints with future timelike one-sided tangents there, and the two tangents at a corner need not agree. If $s$ denotes its parameter and $T_i=dx/ds$ on the $i$th segment, an ideal clock carried along it records the increment

$$\Delta\tau=\frac1c\sum_{i=1}^k\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i}\sqrt{-g(T_i,T_i)}\,ds.$$

The increment is independent of the admissible finite partition, by additivity of the integral, and is additive across corners. On each smooth segment this is the proper-time parameter with $d\tau=c^{-1}\sqrt{-g(dx/ds,dx/ds)}\,ds$. The flat-spacetime specialization is inherited from [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]]; extending that convention to the curved prescribed background is a separate adoption of this framework.

When the parameter $s$ is measured in seconds, $x^0=ct$ is in metres, $c$ is in metres per second, and $\tau$ is in seconds. This is a model postulate, not a theorem or a reported measurement. It does not assert that a physical clock realizes the idealization exactly, that the background solves gravitational field equations, or that the test body affects the background.

## Definition

At an event, for any observer $n$ of [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]], define the spatial momentum and observer energy by

$$q_n(P):=P+g(P,n)n\in n^\perp,\qquad E_n(P):=-c\,g(P,n).$$
